Stamp means to bring something down with force and intention — usually a foot, or a tool, onto a surface. Think of it as an action that is deliberate, firm, and leaves a mark — either a physical one or a lasting impression. That idea of force + intention + mark runs through almost every use of this word.

1. To hit the ground (or a surface) hard with your foot

This is the most basic, everyday meaning. You lift your foot and bring it down with force.

  • She stamped her foot on the floor in frustration.
  • The little boy stamped and screamed when his mother said no.
  • The soldiers stamped their boots as they marched.

Notice that stamping the foot often signals a strong emotion — anger, impatience, or emphasis. It is a physical way of saying "I mean this."

You can also stamp on something, meaning you bring your foot down hard onto it:

  • He stamped on the spider.
  • She stamped on the burning paper to put out the flames.

2. To press a tool onto a surface to make a mark or shape

A "stamp" (the noun) is a tool or device you press down onto something to leave an imprint — like an ink stamp that marks a document, or a machine that presses metal into a shape. When used as a verb, stamp means to use such a tool on something.

  • The officer stamped my passport at the border. (pressed a rubber stamp onto it, leaving an official mark)
  • The librarian stamped the due date inside the book.
  • The factory stamps thousands of metal parts every hour. (a machine presses the metal into the required shape)
  • They stamped the envelope and sent it off. (put a postage stamp on it)

The key idea here is marking or shaping something by pressing down with authority or force.

3. To walk with heavy, loud footsteps

When someone stamps around or stamps across a room, they are walking in a way where their feet hit the ground hard — either out of anger, frustration, or simply because they are a heavy walker.

  • He stamped out of the room, slamming the door behind him.
  • She could hear him stamping up the stairs.
  • The child stamped through the puddles.

4. To permanently mark something (or someone) in a figurative sense — to define or characterize

This is a more abstract use. When an experience, an action, or a quality "stamps" something onto someone, it means it leaves a deep, defining mark on them — not physically, but in terms of identity or memory.

  • His years in the army had stamped him forever. (shaped and defined who he was)
  • The scandal stamped him as a dishonest man. (gave him that permanent reputation)
  • The image was stamped on her memory forever. (she could never forget it)
  • His work clearly stamps him as a master of his craft. (identifies and defines him as one)

Think of it like a brand on cattle — once stamped, the mark stays. When you say something "stamps" a person as a certain type, you mean it definitively identifies them that way in the eyes of others, or in their own experience.
The Most Important Phrasal Verb: Stamp Out

This is one of the most common and important ways "stamp" is used in combination with another word. Stamp out means to completely destroy, suppress, or eliminate something — usually something harmful or undesirable.

The image is vivid: like stamping your foot repeatedly on a small fire until it is fully extinguished.

  • The government is trying to stamp out corruption.
  • Doctors worked to stamp out the disease before it spread further.
  • The teacher stamped out any sign of bullying in the classroom.
  • She stamped out the smouldering ember with her boot.

You will also encounter:

  • Stamp on (figurative) = to suppress something firmly and decisively, often with authority: The manager quickly stamped on the rumour before it spread.

Knowing when to use a word is just as important as knowing what it means. Here are the key tones "stamp" carries:

Force and decisiveness. Stamping is never gentle. It always implies strength, weight, or authority — whether physical or figurative.

Permanence. When something is stamped — a passport, a memory, an identity — it tends to stay. The mark does not easily go away.

Emotion (in physical use). Stamping your foot or stamping around a room almost always signals a strong emotion, most often anger, frustration, or impatience.

Authority (in official use). Officials stamp documents. Factories stamp products. There is an air of finality and legitimacy when something is stamped officially.
A Quick Summary of All Uses

• Foot on floor → to bring the foot down hard, often out of emotion (stamp your foot)
  • Foot on object → to crush or press down on something (stamp on a bug)
  • Walk heavily → to walk with loud, heavy steps (stamp out of a room)
  • Tool on surface → to press a marking tool onto something (stamp a passport, stamp metal)
  • Figurative mark → to define, characterize, or leave a lasting impression on someone (stamped him as a genius, stamped on her memory)
  • Stamp out → to completely eliminate something harmful (stamp out poverty, stamp out a fire)

That is the complete picture of "stamp" as a verb. Every use — physical, official, emotional, or figurative — comes back to that same core idea: a deliberate, forceful action that leaves a mark.
